question: How does the finale turn earlier material and repeated surges into a sense of conclusion?
intro: The finale begins low in the orchestra, but its force soon exceeds the opening movement’s quiet dawn. Turbulent figures alternate with broader lines, earlier material returns, and the ending gathers the whole work toward D♭ major. Follow how the dialogue changes scale rather than assigning each instrument permanently to wind or sea.

sections.label: A · Tumult gathers
sections.mNote: Low-string figures and percussion establish motion before the larger exchanges.

sections.label: B · Broader expansion
sections.mNote: Growing orchestral weight, without a new movement or fixed programme.

sections.label: C · A quieter centre
sections.mNote: Quieter lines leave room after the recorded level falls sharply.

sections.label: D · Renewed weight
sections.mNote: A strong later expansion is followed by another withdrawal.

sections.label: Coda · Final drive
sections.mNote: The closing build carries the movement toward its full-orchestra ending.

cues.title: Motion begins below the surface
cues.text: The finale opens with timpani, low percussion and short low-string figures. Its instruction is animated and tumultuous. Listen for the weight underneath the movement before the higher lines emerge: this opening is already less still than the dawn of the first sketch.
cues.evidence: Durand score p.223 (PDF81), Animé et tumultueux: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/b6/IMSLP15420-Debussy_-_La_Mer_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report rises from the low opening window to a much stronger level around0:10; no individual attack is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A call above the agitation
cues.text: In the early pages, a muted trumpet joins the wind writing above the restless low foundation. Compare a line that can be followed as a phrase with the shorter figures underneath it. Both contribute to the confrontation without needing literal labels for wind and sea.
cues.evidence: Durand score pp.224–225, rehearsal43, shows muted trumpet with oboe and clarinet above low strings and percussion. The report’s0:38 change anchors only the approximate early region.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dialogue, not a literal script
cues.text: Debussy names this sketch a dialogue of wind and sea. The title does not require us to assign one instrument to each speaker. Listen for the changing relationship between short agitated figures and broader phrases, then decide how much of the image you need.
cues.evidence: Movement title in the Durand score; Susan Key’s LA Phil account describes contrasting themes and returning material without a fixed instrument-by-character code: https://www.laphil.com/works/la-mer

cues.title: A surge can fall back quickly
cues.text: The early exchanges already include a substantial crest and a retreat. Keep the phrase in mind as the weight changes: a softer continuation can still belong to the same stretch of musical argument.
cues.evidence: Report: one of the loudest windows is1:10, at −3.5dB; level falls to −15.8 by1:15 and stays lower across much of1:20–1:50. The description is contour-based, not a bar assignment.

cues.title: The broad line needs its background
cues.text: During the larger expansions, listen to what continues underneath the longer phrases. Short repeated figures can sustain pressure while a melody seems to broaden. That separation of timescales helps the finale sound both driven and spacious.
cues.evidence: Durand score movement III, including pp.233–245, juxtaposes sustained wind phrases with moving strings. Report: renewed intensity around2:14 onward locates a broad expansion; no single instrument is isolated by analysis.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The first sketch remains in memory
cues.text: The finale recalls material from the first movement. This is one reason La Mer can act as a connected symphonic design despite its three pictorial titles. Keep the opening movement’s broad ideas in memory rather than listening to this finale as an entirely new scene.
cues.evidence: Susan Key’s LA Phil note explicitly discusses the finale’s recollection of the opening movement: https://www.laphil.com/works/la-mer. This is a work-level relationship, not a claim that the recall begins at3:00.

cues.title: A large crest gives way
cues.text: A powerful central surge has fallen away. The following retreat stretches the distance between this crest and the next one. Notice how the movement creates expectation by withholding the weight that it has already shown it can produce.
cues.evidence: Report:2:50 is the loudest listed five-second window, followed by a fall through3:00–3:10 and lower levels across3:20–3:35. The cue concerns the extended retreat, not a harmonic resolution.

cues.title: Hear the quieter centre as music
cues.text: In this quieter region, listen for the shape of a line and the space around it. Reduced volume does not cancel the movement’s momentum; it changes the scale on which that momentum is heard. Resist listening only for the next full-orchestra entrance.
cues.evidence: Report: a strong3:54 boundary leads to the quietest internal windows at3:55–4:00; levels remain comparatively low through4:30. No precise instrumental entry is inferred from those measurements.

cues.title: The next build begins from less
cues.text: The recorded level begins to rise again after the quiet centre. Follow the whole ascent across several phrases, rather than waiting for one decisive instant. Its size depends partly on the reduced sound from which it starts.
cues.evidence: Report: level rises from about −22dB at4:30–4:35 toward −8.6 at5:00 and −7.2 at5:05, with strong changes at4:42 and5:04. The report supplies the contour only.

cues.title: A historical mono perspective
cues.text: Paray’s Detroit performance reaches us here through a Mercury mono LP transfer, not through the later stereo reissue. The archive documents a modern turntable and digital transfer chain. That chain belongs to this copy’s history; it does not describe the original session’s microphone arrangement.
cues.evidence: IA MG50101 metadata gives the LP transfer chain; Eloquence Mercury Masters vol.1 documents the separate original sessions and later stereo issue: https://www.eloquenceclassics.com/releases-archive/paul-paray-the-mercury-masters-vol-1-1953-1957/. No audible engineering difference is asserted without comparison.

cues.title: Another retreat keeps the ending open
cues.text: After the renewed expansion, the sound has room to gather once more. Listen for how the movement avoids exhausting itself at the earlier crest. A final drive can feel necessary because the preceding release has not sounded like a full stop.
cues.evidence: Report: the5:00–5:15 expansion recedes through5:25–5:55, before the later build. This is a listening interpretation of the measured contour, not an asserted cadence or programme event.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The final course turns toward closure
cues.text: The last broad stretch gathers the orchestra toward its concluding D♭-major destination. Compare its persistent drive with the earlier exchanges that repeatedly opened out and withdrew. The ending has to close the whole three-movement work, not only its own turbulent opening.
cues.evidence: Durand score pp.270–279 supplies the final build and D♭-major ending; LA Phil describes the finale’s closing function. Report: a strong 6:18 change is followed by the rise through 6:30–7:20. Placement is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A final collective statement
cues.text: The final surge gives the orchestra a decisive ending rather than another fading retreat. Listen through the last attacks and their release: the remaining resonance follows a conclusion already made by the players.
cues.evidence: Report:7:20 is among the loudest windows, followed by a sharp fall at7:30. Durand score p.279 ends with full-orchestra attacks and rests. The cue does not identify an exact last attack at7:12.

transitions.title: Short figures support a larger expansion
transitions.how: The low agitation and early exchanges lead into a region with greater sustained weight. Longer lines broaden above continuing motion, so the change does not require the underlying energy to stop. Hear the accumulating sound as an enlargement of the argument rather than a separate episode with a wholly new pulse.
transitions.evidence: Report: strong novelty at2:14 and rising level across2:15–2:50. Durand movement III juxtaposes broader wind lines and persistent short figures; the timestamp identifies a broad listening region, not a specific thematic entrance.

transitions.title: The large swell leaves a quiet opening
transitions.how: The central swell loses its weight over an extended retreat. The quieter centre allows individual lines and their surrounding space to matter again. This is not a new beginning from silence: the movement carries its tension into a different dynamic scale before rebuilding.
transitions.evidence: Report: the2:50 crest recedes, with a further strong change at3:54 and the low internal windows3:55–4:00. The boundary locates the quiet centre only; no chord, cadence or instrument is assigned.

transitions.title: The quiet centre opens into renewed force
transitions.how: A gradual rise carries the music out of the quiet centre into another substantial expansion. The larger orchestral weight arrives as the result of that ascent, not as an unrelated interruption. Listen across the crest and into its later retreat: this is still preparation for the final course rather than the last word.
transitions.evidence: Report: level rises from4:30 toward5:00–5:15;5:04 is the strongest novelty peak in this part of the recording. The prose describes measured broad dynamics, not an exact return of a named theme.

transitions.title: The last rebuilding aims at closure
transitions.how: After another withdrawal, the closing region gathers momentum and orchestral weight. Earlier material is drawn into the finale’s conclusion, and the score drives toward D♭ major rather than allowing one more quiet dispersal. The full-orchestra ending answers the work’s recurring rises and retreats with a decisive release.
transitions.evidence: Durand score pp.270–279 and the LA Phil account of the concluding recollections. Report: strong6:18 change and later increase toward the7:20 crest. No exact bar or cadence is assigned to6:18.

timeline.note: Timpani and low percussion underlie the restless low-string opening.
The early muted-trumpet and wind phrase emerges over low strings and percussion.
The broader early expansion combines wind phrases with persistent string motion.
The quieter central pages expose wind lines and harp figures over softer strings.
The later expansion gives winds and brass greater weight against moving strings.
The following passage rebuilds through shorter wind and string figures.
The final pages bring winds, brass, percussion and strings together for the closing attacks.

composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud

composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
